name: Uptime and redundancy
answer: These measures show how reliably a data center keeps its servers running and connected: network quality, backup power and contractual uptime. An AI training run can last weeks across thousands of chips, so an interruption costs more than in most workloads.

metrics.line: Continuous measurement of round-trip latency, loss rate, and utilization on the facility's internal fabric and external transit.
metrics.label: Network latency, packet loss, and bandwidth

metrics.line: Battery state of health and remaining runtime under current load, and on-site fuel measured in hours of generator operation at load.
metrics.label: UPS battery health and generator runtime

metrics.line: Delivered availability measured against the contracted service level, conventionally quoted in nines.
metrics.label: SLA uptime compliance

reading.body:
Uptime in a data center is measured three ways: network quality, backup power, and contractual availability. The data names the specific signals for each, and they are operational rather than financial.

Network health is tracked as round-trip latency, packet loss, and bandwidth on both the internal fabric and external transit. Backup power is tracked as UPS battery state of health and remaining runtime under current load, plus on-site fuel measured in hours of generator operation at load. Contractual availability is tracked as delivered uptime against the service level, quoted in nines.

The reason these three sit together is the workload. An AI training run can last weeks across thousands of chips, so an interruption costs more than in most workloads. A dropped fabric link or a generator that runs dry mid-run does not just delay a job, it can invalidate the run. That makes redundancy a compute question, not a facilities question.

What the data does not give is any actual figure. There is no latency number, no runtime in minutes, no nines value, and no named facility. It defines what gets measured and why it matters, and stops there.
